pairs.locus: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore 1.6.239-240 (Capitulum VI, visio exercitus mortuorum)
pairs.question: Cuius sit haec quam cerno militia, et quare mulier tam formosa adeo vilem equum et tam sibi abiecta praeelegit vestimenta portare?
pairs.answer: Hic, quem vides, est exercitus mortuorum.
pairs.derivation: Narrator asks the dead lady of the vision an indirect double question; dropped the asking-frame 'Et ego sic respondi: Rogo igitur ut mihi cures, si libet, asserere'. The reply's operative first sentence ('Hic... exercitus mortuorum') directly answers the first interrogative (whose army this is); cut before the following narration 'Quod quum audissem, meus statim ultra modum turbatus est animus'. Normalized capital C and terminal '?'.

pairs.locus: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore 1.6.310-311 (colloquium plebeii et nobilis, B)
pairs.question: Mea namque voluntas esset quae proponitis adimplere, sed cor contradicit omnino et dissuadet per omnia fieri quod plena voluntate desidero. Ergo si cor contradicit amare, cui potius sit favendum, cordi scilicet an voluntati?
pairs.answer: Sed si est quod verbis asseritis, illud prorsus debetis eligere quod iustitia et veritate defenditur.
pairs.derivation: The woman genuinely asks which to follow, heart or will; dropped the asking-frame 'quaeso ut mihi asseratis'. Kept the preceding 'Mea namque voluntas... desidero' so that 'cordi an voluntati' has its referents (self-containment). The man's reply opens with a non-answering remark ('Hanc discordiam me amplius audisse non recolo; quod aliud corde et aliud voluntate quaeratur'), so the answer start is advanced to the operative sentence 'Sed si est quod verbis asseritis...'. Terminal '?' normalized on the question.

pairs.locus: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore 1.6.533-536 (colloquium nobilioris et nobilioris, H)
pairs.question: Nam quum mulier quaedam mirae probitatis industria duorum amorem petentium alterum vellet ex propria electione repellere et alterum prorsus admittere, taliter in se ipsa amoris est partita solatia. Ait enim: 'Alteri vestrum mei sit pars superior electa dimidia, et pars inferior sit alteri designata petenti'. Quorum uterque morae cuiuslibet intermissione reiecta propriam sibi partem elegit, et uterque potiorem se partem elegisse fatetur et altero se digniorem in amoris perceptione pro dignioris partis electione contendit. Praenarrata vero mulier suum nolens improvide praecipitare arbitrium, litigantium consensu, uter istorum sit potior in eo quod postulaverat iudicandus, meo quidem quaerit iudicio definiri. Quaero igitur, quis vobis videatur in sua magis electione laudandus?
pairs.answer: Quis enim dubitat partis eminentioris solatii electorem inferiora praeferendum petenti?
pairs.derivation: The woman lays out a casus (the lady who split herself between two suitors) ending in a real interrogative 'Quaero igitur, quis... laudandus'. Quoted the whole consultation contiguously as the question, dropping only the opening flattery-frame 'Quoniam tamen ex his, quae mecum adinvicem contulistis, vos plurimum exercitatos in amoris doctrina cognosco, super quodam amoris negotio vestrum exquiro consilium'. The reply's whole first paragraph [535] does not answer (it complains of her refusing him: 'Quum a vobis petam amari...'), so the answer start is advanced past it and past the lead-in 'Ad hoc petitis a me vobis super eo consilium exhiberi, super quo neminem decet haesitare prudentem' to the operative rhetorical answer, which delivers the verdict that the chooser of the higher part is to be preferred (developed declaratively in the following 'Ergo inferioris partis elector... admittatur elector'). Terminal '?' on the question normalized.

pairs.locus: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore 1.6.561-562 (colloquium nobilioris et nobilioris, H)
pairs.question: Utrum scilicet amator qui ad aliam accessit feminam, non tamen ipsam amandi vel priorem deserendi affectu, debeat amoris amissione puniri?
pairs.answer: Quum amoris evidenter regula doceatur quod amans pudicitiam tenetur amanti conservare; unde non immerito ex ipsius rationabili intellectu mandati coniicio quod in articulo praesenti amans sit amoris amissione multandus.
pairs.derivation: The man asks an indirect 'utrum... debeat' question; dropped the asking-frame 'rogo ut et vos primitus in quodam mihi sitis in respondendo benigna:' and left out his own appended opinion 'Videtur quod...' (not part of the interrogative). The reply opens with a non-answering preamble ('Nec ego quidem in hoc vobis ero avara responso. Miror tamen cur in hoc vestra potuit prudentia dubitare,'), so the answer start is advanced to the operative 'Quum amoris evidenter regula doceatur...', which answers yes (the lover is to be punished by loss of love). Ended at the full stop after 'multandus' (the trailing ', et sufficere satis credo...' normalized to a period); capital Q normalized.

pairs.locus: Andreas Capellanus, De Amore 1.6.563-564 (colloquium nobilioris et nobilioris, H)
pairs.question: Utrum amoris amissione multetur amator, si ad aliam accessit non amandi affectu, eius tamen nullum habuit voluntas effectum?
pairs.answer: Et iste quoque meretur superiori sententia condemnari, nisi forte poenitudo spontanea delicti et secura omnimoda fidei confirmatio delinquentis animum mitigent coamantis.
pairs.derivation: A second 'utrum... multetur' question; dropped the asking-frame 'Sed adhuc inquietat animum secunda dubitatio talis,' and the man's appended 'Videtur enim quod...' opinion. The reply's first sentence directly answers ('Et iste quoque meretur... condemnari'); cut before the elaborating 'Non enim iuxta praeceptum amoris castitatem videtur amanti servasse...'. Terminal '?' normalized on the question.
